nav.label: Tests
nav.content:
# Tests

This project builds and runs tests from `src/tests` and command-line tools from `src/tools` through the single `src/Makefile`.

## Build and execution model

From `src/`:

```bash
make list
```

This prints the available targets, splitting them into:

- tests: `test_<name>`
- tools: `<tool-name>`

Each target is built automatically from the matching source file:

- `src/tests/test_<name>.cpp` -> test target `<name>`
- `src/tools/<tool>.cpp` -> tool target `<tool>`

Example:

```bash
make utils
make linklayer
make arpup
```

The same pattern is used for all generated binaries under `src/bin/`.

## Compiler settings

The Makefile uses:

```bash
CXX := g++
CXXFLAGS := -std=c++23 -Os -ffunction-sections -fdata-sections -Wl,--gc-sections -fno-exceptions -fvisibility=hidden -s -Wextra -I../include
```

Optional debug build:

```bash
make DEBUG=1 utils
```

This adds `-g -O0` while leaving the normal optimized flags in place.

## Passing arguments to tests/tools

The Makefile supports runtime args via `ARGS`:

```bash
make test_utils ARGS="--help"
make arpup ARGS="-i eth0 -t 192.168.1.10"
```

This is useful for tool invocations and for tests that may accept runtime options.

## Cleanup

```bash
make clean
```

removes the generated binaries from `src/bin/`.

## Practical workflow

Typical local workflow:

```bash
cd src
make list
make utils
make linklayer
```

For tools:

```bash
cd src
make arpup ARGS="-i eth0 -t 192.168.1.10"
```

This project keeps the same test/tool pattern across additions, so new `.cpp` files under `src/tests` or `src/tools` can be added without changing the build conventions.

nav.label: Tools
nav.content:
## ARP `arpup`
___

`arpup` resolves an IPv4 address to a MAC address and prints the result to standard output.

It is intended for quick local network lookups and supports both the kernel ARP cache and a direct ARP request path.

### What it does

- Checks the system/kernel ARP cache for the target IPv4 address.
- If no cached entry is found, optionally sends ARP requests on the selected interface and waits for a reply.
- Prints the MAC address in the format returned by the library.
- Can be used to diagnose neighbor reachability or confirm ARP resolution on a LAN.

### Compile

Change directory into `src`, and run the following command.

```bash
make arpup
```

### Usage

```bash
arpup --interface <iface> --target <ip> [options]
```

### Options

- `-i, --interface <iface>`
  - Interface to use, for example `eth0`, `wlan0`, or `enp3s0`.

- `-t, --target <ip>`
  - Target IPv4 address to resolve, for example `192.168.1.10`.

- `-c, --cache`
  - Use only the kernel ARP cache and do not send an ARP request.

- `-b, --bcast`
  - Force a network ARP request instead of trying the kernel cache first.

- `-m, --timeout <ms>`
  - Timeout in milliseconds for waiting for an ARP reply.

- `-a, --attempts <n>`
  - Number of ARP request attempts before giving up.

### Default behavior

When no explicit mode is selected, `arpup` behaves like this:

1. Try the kernel ARP cache.
2. If the entry is missing, send an ARP request on the selected interface.
3. Wait for a reply and print the resolved MAC.

This makes it useful as a quick fallback lookup path without requiring the user to decide between cache-only and network-based resolution.

### Examples

```bash
./arpup -i eth0 -t 192.168.1.42
./arpup --interface eth0 --target 192.168.1.42 --cache
./arpup -i eth0 -t 192.168.1.42 --bcast
./arpup -i eth0 -t 192.168.1.42 --timeout 500 --attempts 8
```

### Output

Typical output looks like this:

```text
00:11:22:33:44:55 (kernel).
```

or:

```text
00:11:22:33:44:55 (network).
```

# Changelog

All notable changes to this project are documented in this file.

## [1.0.0] - 2026-10-01

### Added

* Initial release of the `lynx` library.
* Header-only C++ interfaces for protocol parsing and object access.
* Core support for buffer management, view handling, error reporting, and configuration types.
* Ethernet frame support, including 802.1Q and QinQ tagging.
* PPP and PPPoE protocol support, including LCP, CHAP, PAP, IPCP, and IPv6CP.
* IPv4, IPv6, ARP, ICMP, ICMPv6, IGMP, TCP, UDP, and SCTP protocol definitions.
* TLV and raw frame helper classes for protocol payload inspection.
* Linux-specific network interface and socket utilities for interface lookup, raw socket creation, and address retrieval.
* Unit tests covering link-layer protocol classification and socket/interface behavior.

### Changed

- No previous release history.

### Fixed

- No fixes recorded for this initial release.

content.name: ARP
content.brief: Address Resolution Protocol (ARP) - Internet Layer classification.

notes.content:
ARP Classification as Internet Layer:
Although ARP is encapsulated inside Ethernet frames (link layer) and is
sometimes classified as a link-layer protocol, it is placed in the Internet
Layer here because:
1. It operates on network-level addresses (IPv4 addresses), not link-layer
2. It is fundamental to IP communication and address resolution
3. It is logically part of the network architecture, not the physical medium
4. This architecture treats IL as all protocols needed for IP-based networking

The EtherType 0x0806 in the Ethernet frame identifies ARP as the payload, making it a peer to IPv4/IPv6 from the media encapsulation perspective.

notes.content: This class deliberately has no field setters beyond construction. Every field after the header is length-prefixed and positional (PAP's Password sits wherever Peer-ID's length says it ends, CHAP's Name wherever Value ends, and so on) - changing one after the fact means shifting every field that follows it, which is a lot of memory movement for comparatively little benefit. content.description: UniInterface binds to a network interface card (NIC) and manages the send and capture lifecycle. It provides methods to open, close, and configure the interface, as well as to resolve MAC addresses via kernel cache.

content.brief: Reference-counted byte buffer.
content.description:
Buffer provides shared storage for packet data while avoiding per-layer allocations and copies. Protocol layers operate on offsets within the same underlying byte slab.

Ownership is shared using `std::shared_ptr<uint8_t[]>`. Buffer inherits BaseObject and reports errors such as BufferTooSmall and BufferAllocFail through its common error state.

notes.content: len() only reflects what write()/reserve() have advanced it to. Writing through a raw pointer obtained via begin()/at() (e.g. handing it to a C API like recvfrom() that has no notion of Buffer) fills memory but does not move len() at all - nothing observes that write happening. If you must write through a raw pointer, use reserve() first to both get the pointer and advance len() by the amount you intend to write, then correct len() (or build the final view yourself from that pointer and the real byte count) once you know how much was actually written, since reserve() has no way to know that in advance.
Buffer does not clean up or zero memory on destruction. Owner/SmartPtr is responsible for that. This is intentional to avoid unnecessary overhead in high-performance packet processing.

content.name: ProtocolBaseObject
content.brief: Common base for every protocol layer (Ether, IPv4, TCP, ...).

notes.content:
Header bytes are stored in network byte order at all times, in both craft and capture mode. A protocol's field accessors are responsible for swapping on every access. If a derived class instead keeps host-order fields and expects a swap-on-serialize step, load() will write the wrong bytes silently, since it has no protocol-specific knowledge to catch that.

A chain is built with operator/, which only links pointers - it does not serialize, checksum, or allocate anything. Bytes are produced once, on demand, by load() into a caller-provided Buffer.

Buffer has fixed capacity - allocate it with size() before calling load(), or just use to_buffer():

- capture: get<T>() default-constructs T, then calls dissect(v) with
a view sliced out of this layer's own payload. No
allocation, no copy - m_origin_view just borrows a slice
of it.
- craft:   a freshly default-constructed object
needs to allocate its own header bytes.

A captured object's origin view aliases the receive buffer it was sliced from. That buffer is typically only guaranteed valid for the duration of the capture scope it was produced in. Chaining a captured object with operator/ and calling load() on it later (e.g. to modify and resend a captured packet) reads through a pointer that may already have been reused by the next captured frame - the object itself is still alive, what it points to is not guaranteed to still hold any data.

Attaching an upper layer with operator/ truncates that object's origin view down to its own header (the first hsize() bytes); any data that previously followed it is no longer reachable through origin(). get<T>() attaches an upper layer through a separate path and does not perform the same truncation, so an object whose upper layer came from get<T>() may still report trailing data through origin() that load() and size() no longer use.

content.name: ~ProtocolBaseObject
content.brief: Destroys the protocol base object.
content.description: Provides a virtual destructor so derived protocol objects can be destroyed correctly through a base-class pointer.

content.name: get
content.brief: Constructs a protocol object from the loaded payload.
content.description: Creates an instance of the requested protocol type and dissects this layer's payload view into it, then links it above this layer (as if by operator/) so m_underlayer_ptr / m_upperlayer_ptr stay consistent for later use (e.g. checksum pseudo-headers).

tparams.name: T
tparams.description: Protocol type to construct. Must derive from ProtocolBaseObject.

notes.content: Only meaningful on a captured object with an un-dissected payload view - see the class-level warning about that view's lifetime before holding onto the result.

return.description: A unique pointer to the constructed protocol object, or `nullptr` if the payload is empty or allocation fails.

content.name: operator/
content.brief: Links this protocol layer with an upper protocol layer.
content.description: Only links m_underlayer_ptr / m_upperlayer_ptr in both directions. Does not serialize, checksum, or copy anything - that happens once, lazily, when load() is eventually called.

notes.content: Assigning an upper layer with operator/ truncates that object's origin view down to its own header (the first hsize() bytes); any data that previously followed it is no longer reachable through origin(). get<T>() attaches an upper layer through a separate path and does not perform the same truncation, so an object whose upper layer came from get<T>() may still report trailing data through origin() that load() and size() no longer use.
Chaining protocols does not alter their properties/header attributes in any way.

params.name: rhs
params.description: Upper protocol layer to attach above this protocol.

return.description: Reference to this protocol layer.

content.name: unload
content.brief: Detaches the upper layer or un-dissected payload from this layer.
content.description:
If `ud` is `true`, detaches any un-dissected payload bytes that remain after this layer's header. If `ud` is `false`, detaches the upper layer (if any) that was linked with operator/ or get<T>().

After this call, size() will return hsize() if `ud` is `true`, or hsize() + whatever trailing bytes remain in m_origin_view if `ud` is `false` and no upper layer was attached.

params.name: ud
params.description: If `true`, detaches un-dissected payload; otherwise detaches the upper layer.

content.name: load
content.brief: Writes this layer and everything chained above it into `buf`.
content.description:
`buf` must already have at least size() bytes of capacity from its current write cursor - Buffer does not grow. Use to_buffer() if you don't want to size and allocate it yourself.

Writes exactly hsize() bytes from the start of m_origin_view, recurses into the linked upper layer (if operator/ or get() attached one), or, if this layer is still holding onto an un-dissected captured remainder past its own header, writes that back out as-is. A crafted layer with no upper layer has nothing past its own header (m_origin_view is exactly hsize() bytes), so that branch is a no-op for it - matches size()'s zero contribution in the same case. Explicit payload attachment (e.g. TCP application data) is not a base concern; that's what a dedicated Raw layer chained on top is for.

Once the full extent belonging to this layer and everything above it has been written, patch() is called with the offset this layer's header started at, so it can read the now- complete bytes and patch its fields in place with buf.patch() - which does not move the write cursor, so this happens safely after the recursive call above has already advanced past this layer's own bytes.

Every Buffer::write() call inside this chain sets an error on `buf` if it runs out of capacity (check buf.ok() afterward); it does not throw or crash.

notes.content: Load set by operator/ is preferred over any un-dissected captured remainder, so if a captured object has an upper layer attached, any trailing bytes in m_origin_view are ignored by load() and size().

params.name: buf
params.description: Buffer to write this layer's serialized bytes into.

content.name: to_buffer
content.brief: Allocates a correctly sized Buffer and writes into it.
content.description: Convenience wrapper around Buffer::alloc(size()) + load().

return.description: A Buffer containing the fully written chain, or one holding status::BufferAllocFail if allocation failed.

content.name: origin
content.brief: Returns this layer's bytes.
content.description: The first hsize() bytes are this layer's header. Anything past that is either an un-dissected captured remainder or, on a crafted object, nothing at all - m_origin_view is exactly hsize() bytes until something is chained above it.

notes.content: If bytes remain past hsize() but operator/ has attached an upper layer, those trailing bytes in origin() are ignored by load()/size() and are effectively dead, even though they are still physically present.

return.description: This layer's origin view.

content.name: payload
content.brief: Returns a view of the protocol payload.

return.description: A non-owning view of the bytes following the protocol header.

content.name: size
content.brief: Returns the total size of this layer and everything above it.
content.description: This is what Buffer::alloc() needs before load() can run, since Buffer does not grow. This layer's header size, plus recursively whatever is chained above it, or - if nothing is chained - whatever's left in m_origin_view past this layer's own header (an un-dissected captured remainder, or nothing at all on a crafted object, where that's always empty).

return.description: Total size in bytes, as load() would produce.

content.name: hsize
content.brief: Returns the header size of this layer.

return.description: Header size in bytes.

content.name: check
content.brief: Validates that the current view is well-formed for this protocol.
content.description: The base implementation checks that the internal view contains at least hsize() bytes. Protocols with additional structural requirements, such as a version field or header-length field, override this method to perform those checks.

notes.content: Minimum requirement is that the view has at least hsize() bytes; additional checks may be protocol-specific.
This method does not set any internal error state; it only returns a boolean indicating validity.

return.description: `true` if the current view is valid for this protocol; `false` otherwise.

content.name: ok
content.brief: Checks whether the protocol object is valid.
content.description: Extends the base object validation by checking that protocol data is available and satisfies the protocol-specific structural requirements.

return.description: `true` if the base object, protocol data, and protocol structure are valid; `false` otherwise.

content.name: error
content.brief: Returns the first error detected by the object.
content.description: Checks the base object state, the protocol view state, and the protocol structure in that order, returning the corresponding error when validation fails.

return.description: The first detected error, or an empty error if the object is valid.

content.name: dissect
content.brief: Dissects raw data into this object's origin view.

notes.content: m_origin_view borrows `v`; no data is copied.
Sets status::BufferTooSmall if `v` is smaller than hsize().

params.name: v
params.description: View containing the raw protocol data. Must contain at least hsize() bytes.

content.name: dissect
content.brief: Allocates and initializes the protocol view.
content.description: Allocates a buffer of the requested size and assigns its ownership and byte span to the protocol object. On invalid input or allocation failure, the object is left in an invalid state and an error is recorded.

content.name: patch
content.brief: Performs post-write validation or modification of this layer.
content.description:
Default implementation performs no operation.

Called by load() after this layer and all upper layers have been written to `buf`. Implementations may inspect or modify the serialized frame, including calculating checksums, validating or correcting addresses, or applying other protocol-specific adjustments.

notes.content: This is a constant method, thus it only patches the serialized bytes in `buf` and does not modify the protocol object's internal state.

params.name: header_offset
params.description: Byte offset in `buf` where this layer's header begins.

content.name: view
content.brief: Non-owning view over a contiguous run of bytes.
content.description: Holds a pointer and a length; never allocates, copies, or frees anything. The memory it points to must outlive the view.

notes.content: view deliberately mirrors std::span's own semantics on one point that's easy to assume is a bug: a const view locks the view (pointer + length) against reassignment, but never locks the bytes it points to - operator[] returns a mutable reference even through a const view, same as std::span<T>. Constness of the bytes themselves is std::span<const T>'s job, which this class does not attempt to provide.

content.name: slice
content.brief: Returns a view of `[begin`, end).

notes.content: Does not check that `begin` <= `end` or that either stays within size(). Values past the end of the actual data produce a view that reports more than is really there.
Two invalid views (carrying error, no matter which) are considered same.

params.description: Index one past the last byte to keep.

return.description: A view over `[begin`, end).

content.name: operator==
content.brief: Compares two views for equality.

return.description: `true` if both views have the same length and the same bytes.

content.name: c_str
content.brief: Reinterprets this view as a C string.

notes.content:
Only valid to read as a string if the view's last byte
is a null terminator. This is a plain reinterpret cast
- it does not check that for you, and reading past the
view's actual data if it isn't null-terminated is
undefined behavior, same as any other unterminated
buffer treated as a string.

return.description: This view's data, reinterpreted as `const` `char*`.

content.name: operator const char*
content.brief: Reinterprets this view as a C string.
content.description:
Equivalent to c_str(), usable via an explicit cast:

```cpp
auto s = static_cast<const char*>(some_view);
```

notes.content: Same precondition as c_str() - only meaningful when the view's last byte is a null terminator.

This operator is not seen by variadic functions like printf: passing a view directly as a %s argument does not invoke it, and reads the view's raw bytes as if they were a pointer instead. Use c_str() explicitly in a printf-style call.

content.name: LYNX_CLOSE_ON_DESTROY
content.brief: Controls whether the network socket is closed on destruction.
content.description:
- `1` - Close the socket in the destructor.
- `0` - Leave the socket open when the object is destroyed.

The default value of `1` provides automatic resource cleanup and prevents file descriptor leaks.

content.name: LYNX_DEFAULT_SNAPLEN
content.brief: Sets the maximum number of bytes captured per frame.
content.description:
A value of `65535` allows complete Ethernet frames to be captured, including jumbo frames.

Lower values can reduce the per-packet copy cost when only packet headers are required.

notes.content: This is a compile-time configuration option.

content.name: LYNX_DEFAULT_TIMEOUT_MS
content.brief: Sets the default receive timeout in milliseconds.
content.description:
Determines how frequently a blocking receive operation wakes up to check the capture stop condition.

Lower values make `stop()` more responsive, while higher values reduce periodic wakeups.

Defaults to `100` milliseconds.

content.name: LYNX_DST_MAC_POLICY
content.brief: Configures the destination MAC address resolution policy.
content.description:
This policy is used by packet transmission functions when no Ethernet frame with an explicit destination MAC address is provided.

Available policies:

- `DST_MAC_BROADCAST`
Always uses the Ethernet broadcast address
`ff:ff:ff:ff:ff:ff`. No ARP lookup is required.

- `DST_MAC_ARP_CACHE`
Resolves the destination MAC address from the destination IPv4 address
using the kernel ARP cache. If no valid ARP cache entry
exists, transmission fails with `Status::ArpResolveFail`.

notes.content: This is a compile-time configuration option.

content.name: LYNX_MAX_READ_RETRIES
content.brief: Maximum number of consecutive receive retries.
content.description: Limits retries for interrupted or temporarily unavailable receive operations before the receive operation fails.

content.name: LYNX_PACKED
content.brief: Marks a structure as packed with no padding between members.
content.description: This macro is used for protocol headers whose on-wire layout must match the binary format exactly.

content.name: LYNX_RECV_BUFFER_SIZE
content.brief: Sets the kernel-side socket receive buffer size in bytes.
content.description:
A larger buffer can reduce packet drops under high traffic at the cost of increased memory usage.

A value of `0` leaves the receive buffer at the kernel default.

notes.content: This is a compile-time configuration option.

content.name: LYNX_SEND_THRESHOLD
content.brief: Maximum number of bytes sent in a single send operation.
content.description: Buffers larger than this threshold are sent in chunks.

content.name: LYNX_SRC_MAC_POLICY
content.brief: Selects the source MAC address resolution policy.
content.description:
Controls which MAC address is placed in the Ethernet source field when Interface automatically wraps a Packet in an EtherFrame.

Supported values:

- `SRC_MAC_IFACE`
Uses the hardware MAC address of the bound network interface.
This is the default and most compatible option.

- `SRC_MAC_RANDOM`
Generates a random locally administered unicast MAC address for each
packet. The locally administered bit is set and the multicast bit is
cleared.

notes.content: This option is only used when the Ethernet source MAC address has not been explicitly provided.

content.name: SRC_MAC_IFACE
content.brief: Use the hardware MAC address of the bound interface.
